description: Two Virginia Tech engineering students focused on space technology, with backgrounds in mechanical engineering, aerospace engineering, and software development. Current involvement includes inspireFly’s CubeSat team and MACHWorks.
summary: Lunar Site Planner, developed by Project Seraphim, helps users compare landing locations, arrival dates, and mission durations for early lunar mission studies. Students, educators, and the public can compare mission options without processing NASA datasets themselves, while engineers can adjust assumptions and inspect the calculations behind each result. Near the Moon’s south pole, terrain can block sunlight needed for solar power or hide Earth, interrupting direct communication. Using NASA’s JPL SPICE geometry and LRO/LOLA terrain data, the application calculates when the Sun and Earth are visible above a location’s terrain horizon. Users can search for scenarios that meet chosen visibility targets, examine the timing and length of outages, and estimate solar generation and battery charge under specified hardware assumptions. Comparing scenarios shows how changing the landing site or schedule affects power availability and opportunities to communicate with Earth. Results can be exported with their inputs and sources for further analysis.
details:
Project Seraphim’s Lunar Site Planner is a browser application for comparing lunar landing locations, arrival dates, and mission durations. It calculates when terrain blocks the Sun or Earth, identifies continuous periods of darkness and lost Earth visibility, and estimates solar generation and battery charge under adjustable hardware assumptions. A site can receive sunlight for most of a mission and still have a continuous shadow interval long enough to drain the lander’s battery.

Users select coordinates on a 3D Moon or enter them directly, then choose a landing date and mission duration. They can analyze a fixed mission or search across locations, landing dates, and a specified duration range. Search targets include minimum sunlight and Earth-visibility percentages and maximum continuous outage durations. The application returns up to five sampled matches and supports comparisons of up to twelve scenarios. CSV exports record results and modeling assumptions; JSON exports also include the source-reference register.

The geometry pipeline uses NASA/JPL’s DE440 ephemerides and lunar orientation kernels through SPICE, accessed in Python with SpiceyPy. Preprocessing calculates hourly Sun and Earth position vectors in the MOON_ME_DE440_ME421 lunar reference frame, which aligns DE440 orientation with the Mean-Earth frame used by the terrain products. SPICE applies light-time and stellar-aberration corrections to account for light travel time and the observer’s motion. The browser interpolates the Moon-centered vectors, subtracts the surface observer’s position, and projects the resulting directions into local east, north, and up coordinates to calculate azimuth and elevation. NASA’s SPICE documentation defines these corrections.

Terrain calculations use elevation products from the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter’s Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter, or LOLA. The shipped south-polar site profiles use an 80-meter-per-pixel elevation grid, with a 240-meter grid extending coverage. Preprocessing samples great-circle rays at 0.5-degree azimuth intervals, extending approximately 600 kilometers where elevation data are available. It accounts for lunar curvature and records the highest apparent terrain elevation in each direction, producing a skyline around an observer positioned two meters above the modeled surface. NASA’s LOLA product documentation specifies the elevation grids and coordinate system. Outside the polar grids’ coverage, terrain calculations can use the global LOLA raster distributed through NASA’s CGI Moon Kit. Its grid spacing is approximately 1.9 kilometers at the equator, so it cannot resolve small local obstructions.

The sunlight percentage measures the fraction of mission time when any part of the solar disk clears the terrain horizon. Solar generation also depends on how much of the disk remains exposed. Partial exposure uses a circular-segment approximation that treats the skyline as straight across the Sun. Earth visibility requires Earth’s center to exceed a user-selected clearance above the terrain. NASA’s published polar visibility maps instead count Earth as visible when any portion of its disk clears the horizon. Those maps provide comparison data; the application calculates each mission’s visibility from its selected coordinates and dates. NASA explains the map convention in its lunar polar illumination documentation.

The power model calculates electrical output from solar irradiance, panel area, conversion efficiency, panel orientation, and the visible fraction of the solar disk. Irradiance follows the inverse-square relationship with Sun distance. Users can compare a Sun-tracking array, a vertical array that rotates toward the Sun, and a fixed horizontal array. The battery calculation integrates generation minus a constant electrical load, limits stored energy to the selected capacity, and records minimum charge, the onset and duration of unmet demand, total unmet energy, and generation that cannot be used or stored. Batteries begin fully charged and assume 100% charging and discharging efficiency. Demonstration defaults use a 2-square-meter array, 28% efficiency, a 150-watt load, and a 1,500-watt-hour battery. Under these assumptions, the fully charged battery supplies the default load for ten hours without solar input.

Final mission summaries use 15-minute calculation intervals, with additional 5-minute probes near detected horizon crossings and partial solar exposure. Charts and exported time series retain hourly display samples and the mission endpoints. This separates the numerical integration interval from the display interval, although brief events between calculation probes can still be missed. Synchronized horizon and timeline views show how the Sun or Earth moves behind terrain during an interruption. The globe provides geographic context; its viewing light operates separately from the scientific visibility calculation.

Search evaluates a bounded set of locations, dates, and durations, screens candidates at coarser time intervals, and recalculates a shortlist using the final mission method. An unrestricted location search includes points distributed across a Fibonacci sphere and the shipped terrain sites. A radius-constrained search samples the center and two surrounding rings. Duration ranges sample up to eight lengths. Ranking first considers whether a scenario meets the selected targets, then compares normalized target shortfalls and the sum of the separate sunlight and Earth-visibility fractions. Simultaneous visibility is reported as a separate metric. Search does not establish a globally optimal landing site. Nine shipped sites and 49 default search-grid locations have precomputed terrain profiles. Uncached coordinates retain an explicitly identified flat-horizon estimate unless the optional Python terrain service supplies a profile for the requested coordinates.

We built the interface with React, TypeScript, HTML, and CSS, using Three.js for the Moon and KaTeX for equations. Vite and Node.js/npm handle development and production builds. Python preprocessing uses NumPy for numerical operations, Rasterio for elevation rasters, pyproj for coordinate transformations, and SpiceyPy for SPICE calculations. Requests downloads source files, and Pillow processes image assets. Vitest and pytest support verification. NASA’s GSFC/LRO Moon model supplies the globe, and a filtered Yale Bright Star Catalog hosted by NASA HEASARC supplies the background stars; neither enters the mission calculations. Git and GitHub track source changes, and Vercel hosts the application. OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude assisted development.

Precomputed binary and JSON files allow the shipped analyses to run in a browser with WebGL 2 support, without an external database or API key. Browser localStorage retains comparison selections. Python and the source elevation rasters are required to regenerate datasets or calculate uncached terrain profiles. This deployment choice reduces setup for users while limiting static hosting to the terrain profiles already supplied. Search periodically yields control to the browser to keep the interface responsive during calculation.

Verification covers individual calculations and complete mission results. Stored checks compare interpolated geometry with direct SPICE evaluations, mission summaries with one-minute calculations, terrain profiles with finer sampling, and battery behavior with a separate Python numerical integration. An exhaustive 147-scenario reference checks shortlist results within a defined search space. The recorded mission-level report passed the team’s numerical budgets across six geographic holdouts and three additional polar regression cases. It also retains threshold-sensitive disagreements: small numerical differences can change a pass/fail result when a target equals the calculated value. Published-map comparisons remain contextual because terrain versions and simulation epochs differ.

The shared timeline lets users compare shadow intervals, solar generation, and battery charge, then test another landing date or panel configuration. Students and educators can investigate why nearby locations or different arrival dates produce different results. Teams conducting preliminary mission studies can compare candidate scenarios and export their assumptions and results for further analysis. Bringing these calculations into one browser workspace lets users examine their relationships without assembling separate mapping, ephemeris, and power-analysis programs.

Development required tradeoffs between terrain detail, calculation time, browser responsiveness, and deployment complexity. We kept sourced data, calculated results, and assumed hardware parameters distinguishable so users can identify what drives a result. Earth visibility represents geometric line of sight; communication capability still requires a radio link budget and ground-station analysis. The battery model omits storage losses, thermal effects, and degradation. Terrain features smaller than the source grids can be missed, and numerical refinement cannot recover missing terrain detail. Landing hazards and thermal survival require separate analyses.
